stops.name: Burial at Coupvray, home to the vines (10 January 1852)
stops.campa: They carry him back to Coupvray, and on the tenth of January he is laid in the old village cemetery at the top of the town, beside his father Simon-René and his sister, in the sixth row, in the middle. The vines he was born among close over him. It is a small country funeral for a man the world has not yet learned to name. For a hundred years he will lie here quietly while, city by city and nation by nation, the alphabet he made rises out of obscurity and conquers the earth, until France comes at last to fetch him home to her greatest dead.

stops.name: The pupils keep the code; France adopts braille (1854)
stops.campa: Two years after his death, the pressure the blind pupils have never ceased to exert breaks through: the Institute officially adopts the system, and France with it. The underground alphabet, the one written with forks and needles against a director's fire, becomes the sanctioned script of the blind of France. The children who kept it alive have won the argument by simply refusing to read anything else. Louis, in the Coupvray earth, is vindicated in the only court that mattered, the fingers of those he taught.

stops.name: The world after: the alphabet crosses the earth
stops.campa: From France the dots spread outward through the whole blind world. Dr. Thomas Rhodes Armitage carries the cause to the first European congress of blind educators; nation after nation takes up the six-point cell, until it is the common script of the sightless everywhere. English, Chinese, Arabic, mathematics, chemistry, the whole of music, all bend to fit within the two-by-three cell a French boy folded from a soldier's cipher. What was, at his death, the private code of a few hundred pupils becomes the universal literacy of the blind of the earth, and stays, essentially unchanged, to this day.

stops.name: The monument at Coupvray, the village claims its son (1887)
stops.campa: The village that buried a country schoolmaster now raises a monument to a benefactor of mankind. In the Parc de l'Harmonie the sculptor Étienne Leroux sets a stone Louis Braille three metres and more in height on a white base; the perpetual grant on his grave is decreed. Coupvray understands at last whom it bore. Pilgrims of the blind begin to come to the birth-house among the vines, to lay their fingers on the workshop bench and the awl, to read in dots the name of the man who gave them reading. The forgotten grave has become a shrine.

stops.name: The exhumation, the hands cut off and kept (18–20 June 1952)
stops.campa: For the centenary France resolves to bear him to the Panthéon, and Coupvray will not give up all of him. On the eighteenth of June the grave is opened. The town council keeps his hands: the hands that read, that punched the dots, that ran the organ manuals, that first felt the six-point cell at a single touch. They are sealed in an urn under an inscription: the commune devoutly preserves in this urn the hands of the genius inventor. The body goes to Paris; the fingers stay in the vine-country soil that made them, divided as a relic is divided, so both places may keep him.
stops.quote: The commune of Coupvray devoutly preserves in this urn the hands of the genius inventor.
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the reliquary urn of Louis Braille's hands, Coupvray cemetery (1952)

stops.name: The Panthéon, the ashes borne among the great of France (22 June 1952)
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of June the coffin is carried through Paris to the Panthéon, and behind it walk hundreds of the blind, tapping their white canes against the stone: a river of the sightless following their maker to the temple of the nation's dead. At the Sorbonne the world's dignitaries gather, and Helen Keller, deaf and blind, gives the address for all who read by touch. Louis Braille is laid among Voltaire and Rousseau and Hugo, one hundred years from the quiet country grave. The forgotten schoolmaster of Coupvray is now, forever, one of the immortals. Only his hands are absent, kept among the vines.

stops.name: The cell facing the knots: braille, Labanotation, and the quipu
stops.campa: The six-dot cell rests at the center of a family of scripts written to the hand and not the eye. Barbier's twelve-dot cipher of the soldiers, the boy's fold to six; Laban's staff of movement set down; and older and farther, the knotted cords of the quipu, where meaning lives in the fingers of the reader counting knots along the string. All are the same wager: that the mind may be reached through touch, that a code held in the hand can carry a whole world. Braille's fingers, kept at Coupvray, are kin to the knot-readers of the Andes: both proved that to read, the eye is not required.
